title: Containers, iterators and algorithms

objectives.text: Use vector capacity/size and iterator invalidation rules to mutate/erase safely without retaining invalid element/end observers.
Choose an order/duplicate-preserving representation and apply a strict-order stable algorithm without silently changing identity, tie or caller-mutation policy.

blocks.markdown: Choose a container from the data contract before guessing at speed. An ordinary std::vector<T> (excluding the specialized vector<bool>) is a contiguous dynamic sequence that preserves order and repeated values; it is a natural starting point for a small replay/snapshot sequence. A unique-key associative map stores at most one value per key, so a construction/assignment keyed only by a repeated trade label can lose multiplicity. A set represents uniqueness, not a counted event log. Stable business identity and chronological ordering are separate metadata, not properties inferred from a container type. This lesson uses synthetic labels, not authenticated execution IDs.

vector.size() counts constructed elements; capacity() counts storage available before growth requires reallocation. reserve(n) may increase capacity but does not create elements or change size. Indexing a reserved-but-unconstructed slot is not made valid by capacity. For this lesson, use at(i) for checked element access; an out-of-range access raises std::out_of_range rather than supplying a valid missing value. Do not read or write end(): it is a one-past position, not an element.

An iterator is a position/access mechanism under a container-specific validity contract, not a permanent business identifier. For vector, capacity-changing reserve invalidates all element iterators/references/pointers and end(); reserve without capacity change does not. push_back with reallocation invalidates all; without reallocation it still invalidates the old end(). erase invalidates the erased position and everything at/after it, including end(). Sorting can permute values even if storage remains, so a still-dereferenceable slot need not denote the same business record. Reacquire positions from current valid state; do not probe an invalid old iterator to see whether the bytes survived.

blocks.title: Erase without stepping through an invalid iterator

steps.text: Start [1,2,3,4] at begin(). Keep 1 and increment. On 2, erase returns the next valid position now holding 3; assign that return to it, without incrementing the invalid old iterator.
Keep 3 and increment. On 4, erase returns the updated end(); the next condition ends the loop. Survivors [1,3] keep their original order.
A naive erase(it); ++it uses an invalidated iterator and can skip values or have undefined behavior. This explanation does not execute that invalid program.

blocks.caption: Expected output: 2, 2, 3, 1, 3, 5 on separate lines. After removal size is 2; reserve(16) leaves it 2. at(1) reacquires the current second value 3. Adding 5 then iterating current begin/end is safe. No address/capacity growth factor or stale-iterator behavior is assumed.

blocks.markdown: The explicit single-erase loop makes validity easy to trace, but repeated vector erases can shift many elements and cost quadratic time in total. For bulk filtering, erase-remove or C++20 std::erase_if can compact once under their contracts. Do not claim all vector operations are constant time: element access is constant time, end insertion is amortized constant time, and arbitrary middle erase/insertion shifts elements. reserve can reduce reallocations when a useful bound is known, but reserving exact next size before every append can defeat geometric growth. Measure realistic use rather than swapping containers on slogans.

Algorithms require more than a compilable callable. Sorting comparison must define a strict weak ordering: a<a is false; if a<b then not b<a; ordered comparisons and equivalence classes must be consistent/transitive. The integer price comparator below uses <, not <=. Equal-price elements are equivalent under that comparator. stable_sort preserves their original relative order; std::sort does not promise that tie preservation. Stability is a declared snapshot policy, not a claim that a venue uses price-time priority or that a repeated label is a retried fill.

blocks.caption: Expected lines: T2:10, T1:10, T1:20, T1:20, 3. The first three lines are the stable sorted copy; equal-price T2 precedes the later T1. The fourth confirms the original first record is unchanged. All 3 records survive, including repeated labels. No map overwrite, deduplication, live book or execution guarantee is implied.

blocks.markdown: Do not retain raw element pointers across mutations unless the exact operation/type contract proves them valid. Node-based and hash containers have different iterator/reference rules, ordering guarantees, memory costs and performance profiles; choose/read those contracts before substituting one. For persistence or parallel mutation, synchronization, versioned identity and durable replay are additional requirements. This lesson is a single-threaded in-memory demonstration.

Independent transfer: filter a vector with no matches, all matches and adjacent even values, checking survivor order and size. Replace the repeated-erase implementation with C++20 std::erase_if and compare outputs, without dereferencing stale iterators. Sort a snapshot with many equal prices and repeated labels, proving multiplicity, stable ties, sortedness and original immutability separately. Explain why changing < to <= violates the comparator contract even if one small run appears sorted.

Sources: [vector contracts](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector.html), [erase and returned iterator](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector/erase.html), [reserve](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector/reserve.html), and [stable_sort](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/stable_sort.html). Ordinary successful single-threaded operations are used; allocation/throwing element operations and other containers need their own reviewed exception/validity contracts.

summary: Containers carry ordering, duplication, mutation and invalidation contracts. Preserve identity/multiplicity, reacquire valid vector positions after mutation, and use a strict-order comparator with an explicit tie policy rather than trusting a plausible sorted output.
